notes: Podium expert rules. Thresholds come from our domain experts; tune them here, never in code. Condition and fact reference: knowledge_base/FACTS.md.

then.why: Over 170 words per minute is hard for listeners to follow, and it reads as nervous.
then.tip: Slow down to about 140 to 160 words per minute. Land each key point, then breathe.
then.drill: Read your opening out loud with a metronome at 140 beats per minute, one word per beat.

then.why: Under 110 words per minute can sound unsure or unprepared, and the audience drifts.
then.tip: Pick up the pace a little and cut long setups. Know your next sentence before you finish this one.
then.drill: Say your main point in 30 seconds, then in 20, then in 15.

then.why: More than 5 fillers a minute makes you sound less sure of what you're saying.
then.tip: When you feel an 'um' coming, close your mouth and pause instead. Silence sounds confident.
then.drill: Talk about your topic for 60 seconds while a friend taps the table at every filler. Aim for zero taps.

rules.name: Pauses that sound like you lost your place

then.why: Long stops in the middle of a sentence sound like you forgot what comes next.
then.tip: Finish the sentence, then pause. Keep a 3 to 5 word outline of each section in your head.
then.drill: Write one keyword per section on a card and practice moving from card to card without stopping mid sentence.

then.why: Without pauses between ideas, nothing stands out and the audience can't absorb your points.
then.tip: Pause for a full second after each key point and before your big lines.
then.drill: Mark a slash in your script after every key sentence and hold a silent count of two at each one.

then.why: Your pitch barely moves (under 20 Hz of variation), which makes even great content sound flat.
then.tip: Let your voice rise on questions and exciting moments, and drop it for serious ones.
then.drill: Read one paragraph three times: as a bedtime story, as a sports announcer, then somewhere in between.

rules.name: Trailing off at the end of sentences

then.why: Your volume drops at the end of many sentences, and the last words are usually the important ones.
then.tip: Keep your energy all the way through the last word, as if it's the punchline.
then.drill: Say each sentence of your opening and slightly stress the final word.

then.why: The transcriber was unsure about many of your words, which usually means mumbling or swallowed endings.
then.tip: Open your mouth a little more and finish the consonants at the ends of words.
then.drill: Read a paragraph with a pen held lightly between your teeth, then read it again without it.

then.why: You faced the camera less than 60% of the time. People trust speakers who look at them.
then.tip: Treat the camera lens as a person's eyes. Glance away to think, then come back.
then.drill: Put a small sticker next to your webcam and finish every sentence looking at it.

then.why: Your hands were still or out of frame over 80% of the time. Gestures make you look relaxed and help people follow.
then.tip: Keep your hands in frame at waist height and use them to show size, lists, and contrasts.
then.drill: Practice one section where every main point gets a gesture: count on fingers, show big vs small.

then.why: You rocked side to side several times every 10 seconds, which pulls attention away from your words.
then.tip: Plant your feet hip width apart and only move with a purpose, like stepping forward for a key point.
then.drill: Practice your opening standing on a sheet of paper without letting your feet slide.

then.why: Phrases like 'I think maybe' and 'sorry' undercut your authority.
then.tip: Say what you know directly. Replace 'I think we could' with 'We will'.
then.drill: Write out your three main points with no qualifiers, then say them out loud exactly as written.

then.why: An answer over 2 minutes loses the interviewer. Most strong answers land in 60 to 90 seconds.
then.tip: Use the STAR format: Situation, Task, Action, Result, about one or two sentences each.
then.drill: Retell your longest answer in STAR format with a 90 second timer running.

rules.name: No clear ask at the end

then.why: There was no call to action in your last 20%, so listeners don't know what you want from them.
then.tip: End with one specific ask: an amount, a meeting, a sign up, or a next step.
then.drill: Write your ask in one sentence with a number in it, and make it the last thing you say.

then.why: Fast pace plus frequent fillers is the classic sign of nerves.
then.tip: You're likely nervous and rushing. Take one slow breath before you start, and pause after each main point.
then.drill: Read your first paragraph at half speed three times.

then.why: At least one of your metrics improved by more than 15% since your last take.
then.tip: Whatever you changed is working. Keep it up.

then.why: You were looking down over 40% of the time, which usually means reading.
then.tip: Know your key points well enough to glance at slides only for cues.
then.drill: Practice each slide by saying its key point from memory before looking at it.

then.why: Your first 15 seconds had no hook: no question, number, or story to pull people in.
then.tip: Open with a surprising number, a question, or a 2 sentence story.
then.drill: Write three different first sentences and try each out loud. Keep the one that makes you lean in.

then.why: You rushed and skipped the hook, which means the first impression is where the nerves hit hardest.
then.tip: Memorize your first two sentences word for word and say them slowly. The rest gets easier.
then.drill: Record just your first 20 seconds five times in a row until it feels calm.

then.why: Three or more hedges ('I think', 'maybe', 'probably') weaken your claims in a debate.
then.tip: State claims directly, then back them with evidence. Save qualifiers for when you truly concede a point.
then.drill: Take your main argument and say it as one sentence that starts with 'The evidence shows'.

then.why: Most of your answers were missing part of the Situation, Task, Action, Result story, often the result.
then.tip: End every behavioral answer with the result, ideally with a number.
then.drill: For your top 3 stories, write one line each for Situation, Task, Action, and Result.

then.why: You went more than 10% over your time limit. In the real thing you'd get cut off.
then.tip: Cut your weakest section entirely rather than rushing through everything.
then.drill: Time each section separately and trim the longest one by a third.

then.why: You used less than 60% of your time, so there's room to go deeper.
then.tip: Add one example or story to your most important point.
then.drill: For each main point, add one 'for example' sentence.

then.why: Your face stayed very still and you rarely smiled, so your words carried less warmth.
then.tip: Smile when you greet the audience and let your face react to your own story.
then.drill: Practice in front of a mirror and smile on purpose at your opening and closing lines.

then.why: Your voice was quiet in the recording, which makes you sound less confident.
then.tip: Project to the back of the room, from your belly rather than your throat.
then.drill: Practice your opening as if the listener is across the street, then bring it down halfway.

then.why: A slow, flat delivery makes it hard for investors to believe you're excited about your own idea.
then.tip: Stand up, speed up a little, and let your voice rise when you talk about what makes this big.
then.drill: Pitch your idea to a friend in 30 seconds as if you just found out you won.

then.why: You spoke at a comfortable pace that's easy to follow.
You used very few filler words, so you sound prepared and sure.
You paused between ideas, which gives your points room to land.
You looked at your audience most of the time, which builds trust.
Your pitch moved naturally, which keeps people listening.
You stated things directly with no hedging.
You used your hands naturally to support what you said.
You closed with a clear call to action.
Your answers were focused and followed a clear story structure.
